bib.title: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens", Jesse Mu, Xiang Lisa Li, Noah Goodman (Stanford University). NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems); arXiv:2304.08467v3, 12 Feb 2024. Code/data/checkpoints: https://github.com/jayelm/gisting

COVERAGE: 26 of 26 pages; the extraction is 84,897 chars. I read chars 0-62,000 in full (main text, references, appendices A-F, Listing A.1/A.2, Tables A.1/A.2). From 62,000 to the end I read only the first ~9,000 chars (Examples 1-6 of Listing A.3) and skimmed the rest. That part is non-cherry-picked model-output examples, with no new results. Figures were not rendered; I used the captions and the text only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Gisting trains an LM to compress a prompt into k "gist" tokens by changing only the attention mask. Tokens after the gist cannot attend to the prompt. Training costs nothing extra over standard instruction finetuning.
 number: none
 setup: single gist token g added to the vocabulary; input is (t, g1..gk, x). Decoder-only models mask out the lower-left corner of the causal mask. Encoder-decoder models also mask the encoder and the decoder cross-attention.
 quote: "This allows a model to learn prompt compression and instruction following at the same time, with no additional training cost." Also: "these masking changes are extremely simple and can be implemented in roughly 10 source lines of code."
 where: p.2 (Sec 1), p.4 (Sec 3)
2. Up to 26x prompt compression with output quality close to the uncompressed positive control, on unseen tasks.
 number: 26x; win rates vs positive control are 48.6/50.8 (Seen), 49.7/46.2 (Unseen), 45.8/42.5 (Human OOD) for LLaMA-7B / FLAN-T5-XXL
 setup: single-gist-token models trained on Alpaca+ (130,321 examples; 104,664 unique tasks). ChatGPT-3.5 pairwise judge against the positive control, where 50% means parity. The 26x figure is on the Human split, whose average prompt is ~26 tokens.
 quote: "On Unseen prompts within the Alpaca+ distribution, we again see competitive performance: 49.7% (LLaMA) and 46.2% (FLAN-T5) win rates against the positive controls. It is on the most challenging OOD Human split where we see slight drops in win rate to 45.8% (LLaMA) and 42.5% (FLAN-T5)"
 where: p.5 (Sec 5), Table 1 p.6
3. Table 1 (single gist token). ROUGE-L, Pos / Gist / TF-IDF / Neg.
 number: LLaMA-7B Seen 58.0 / 57.8 / 38.1 / 31.5; Unseen 48.1 / 46.6 / 34.0 / 31.4; Human 27.0 / 23.9 / 16.5 / 14.4. FLAN-T5-XXL Seen 50.6 / 48.9 / 32.0 / 25.5; Unseen 45.7 / 43.8 / 34.3 / 29.1; Human 23.9 / 21.7 / 13.5 / 12.4. ChatGPT win rate for LLaMA Human: Gist 45.8, TF-IDF 24.6, Neg 22.2.
 setup: as in claim 2. Positive control = standard instruction finetuning. Negative control = no access to the task. TF-IDF = one keyword subword per instruction.
 quote: "LLaMA- Pos 58.0 (100) 50.0 (100) 48.1 (100) 50.0 (100) 27.0 (100) 50.0 (100) 7B Gist 57.8 (99.2) 48.6 (92.4) 46.6 (91.0) 49.7 (98.8) 23.9 (75.4) 45.8 (84.9)"
 where: p.6
4. Discrete compression (keep one keyword) is far worse than gisting. It is only marginally above the negative control.
 number: LLaMA Human ChatGPT 24.6% (TF-IDF) vs 22.2% (Neg) vs 45.8% (Gist)
 setup: TF-IDF keyword, first subword token only, same compression rate as 1 gist token
 quote: "gist compression is vastly superior to discrete compression; the TF-IDF models in Table 1 only marginally outperform the negative control models across the board."
 where: p.5
5. The number of gist tokens barely matters. One token is enough, and 10 can hurt.
 number: k in {1, 2, 5, 10}; compression factors up to 26x/13x/5x/3x on the Human split
 setup: both models, Figure 3
 quote: "Models were generally insensitive to the number of gist tokens k: compressing prompts into a single token prefix did not substantially underperform larger prefixes. In fact, having too many gist tokens hurts performance in some cases (e.g. LLaMA-7B, 10 gist tokens), perhaps because the increased capacity enables overfitting to the training distribution."
 where: p.5
6. Efficiency: 40% FLOPs saving and 4-7% wall-time saving versus no caching. Gain over plain KV-cache of the instruction is small.
 number: LLaMA CUDA time 23.4 ms (None) / 22.1 (Instruction cache) / 21.8 (Gist), saving 6.8% vs None and 1.0% vs Instruction. GFLOPs 915 / 553 / 552: 40% vs None, 0.11% vs Instruction. FLAN-T5 31.0 -> 29.7 ms (4.2%), 716 -> 427 GFLOPs (40%).
 setup: single forward pass (one decode step, one input token), PyTorch 2.0, 1xA100, averaged over the 252 Human instructions. Average KV cache length is 26 for instruction caching and 1 for gist.
 quote: "Gist caching improves significantly over unoptimized models, with 40% FLOPs savings and 4-7% lower wall time for both models." and "a negligible decrease in FLOPs (0.11%) and a modest 1% speedup in wall time."
 where: p.8 (Table 3, Sec 6)
7. The main practical win over ordinary KV-cache reuse is storage and context space, not FLOPs. About 26x more cached prompts fit in the same storage.
 number: 1.05 MB per token of KV cache for LLaMA-7B; 26x more prompts
 setup: fp32; 4 bytes x 2 (K+V) x 32 layers x 32 heads x 128 head dim (footnote 3)
 quote: "for LLaMA-7B, each token in the KV cache requires 1.05 MB storage." and "gisting allows caching of up to 26x more prompts than full instruction caching, using the same amount of storage!"
 where: p.8
8. Why FLOPs barely drop versus instruction caching: a forward pass is dominated by processing the new tokens, not by attention over the KV cache.
 number: ~10% (at most 9.6%) of per-layer attention FLOPs depend on KV cache size at 2000 tokens. Predicted gist gain 0.12% vs observed 0.11%.
 setup: Chinchilla FLOPs equations modified for KV cache length; LLaMA-7B, 2000-length cache, single input token
 quote: "a forward pass through LLaMA-7B with a single input token and a 2000-length KV cache is only ~10% more expensive than the same forward pass with no KV cache" and "the Chinchilla equations predict a relative improvement of Gist caching of 0.12%. This is extremely close to the 0.11% improvement actually observed in Table 3."
 where: p.8, App F p.16-18
9. Human evaluation agrees with ChatGPT as judge, though inter-annotator agreement is low.
 number: human vs ChatGPT average win rate 52.3 vs 48.0 (LLaMA) and 40.6 vs 42.0 (FLAN-T5). Cohen's kappa among humans .24 / .33; ChatGPT vs humans .29 for both.
 setup: 100 of 252 Human-split examples, 3 Prolific annotators each (US/UK), ~10% "I Don't Know" dropped. Humans cost $141.64; ~22.5k ChatGPT judgments cost $29.28.
 quote: "human annotators agree with ChatGPT, with average win rates of 52.3% (vs. 48.0%) for LLaMA-7B and 40.6% (vs. 42.0%) for FLAN-T5-XXL."
 where: p.5-7 (Table 2), App C-D p.15-16
10. Gist outputs often differ from the positive control's. Exact match is high only on seen tasks.
 number: ~50% on Seen, ~20-25% on Unseen, ~10% on Human
 setup: exact string match, single-token gist vs positive control (Fig A.3)
 quote: "for Seen tasks (but unseen inputs), the gist model outputs exactly match the positive control nearly 50% of the time. This drops to ~20–25% for Unseen tasks and ~10% for the OOD Human tasks."
 where: p.7
11. Failure modes: loss of specific detail (verbatim phrases) and runaway generation.
 number: none
 setup: Human split examples. FLAN-T5 gist output "Culture" instead of the listed category "Arts & Culture". LLaMA gist output a LaTeX example that repeats "\subparagraph{The Basics}" for hundreds of tokens.
 quote: "first, when the instruction contains specific details, e.g. phrases that must be copied verbatim into the output" and "We also see more cases of runaway generations that do not occur with the positive control model"
 where: p.7 (Sec 5.1)
12. Encoder-decoder (FLAN-T5) generalises slightly worse out of distribution than decoder-only (LLaMA).
 number: Human ChatGPT win rate 42.5 vs 45.8; normalised score 63.2 vs 84.9
 setup: the paper's hypothesis is untested
 quote: "one possible reason is that gist masking inhibits the bidirectional attention flow in the encoder, which is more challenging to adjust to than simply limiting the history of a decoder LM. Future work will be needed to investigate this hypothesis."
 where: p.7

LIMITS
- The authors concede: "achieving such compression necessarily results in some loss of nuance of the original instruction". They tell practitioners to evaluate the compute/accuracy tradeoff before deployment.
- The method needs finetuning the LM itself. Retrofitting a frozen LM with a separate compressor is listed only as future work. The same goes for compressing very long prompts such as k-shot, and for "gist pretraining".
- Prompts are short, about 20-26 tokens. The paper never tests long contexts, multi-turn history or documents. Its own future-work section says the biggest gains would come from long prompts.
- The only models are LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL (11B). Training data is synthetic Alpaca+ from GPT-3 davinci. About 59% of tasks have no input.
- Quality is judged by ChatGPT-3.5 and 100 examples with 3 humans. Cohen's kappa is low (.24-.33). ROUGE-L is also used. There are no downstream task benchmarks.
- Wall-time gains are measured on single-step decoding at small scale; the authors expect larger gains with bigger sequences and batches, but do not measure that.
- Dated: the models and judge (LLaMA-1, ChatGPT-3.5 from Mar-Apr 2023) are old. Context windows have grown a great deal since, so the context-space motivation reads differently. This is my inference, not the paper's.
- Instruction caching (the "Instruction" column) does not apply to T5-style encoder-decoders. Gisting is what enables prompt caching there.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Prefix-tuning (Li and Liang, 2021); prompt-tuning (Lester et al., 2021); adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019); LoRA (Hu et al., 2022); context distillation (Askell et al., 2021; Snell et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022); Wingate et al. (2022) prompt compression into a soft prompt; HyperNetworks (Ha et al., 2017); HyperTuning (Phang et al., 2022); Compressive Transformer (Rae et al., 2020); sparse and sliding-window attention (Beltagy et al., 2020; Child et al., 2019); instruction tuning (Wei et al., 2022); Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2022); Stanford Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023); LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023); FLAN-T5 (Chung et al., 2022); Pope et al. (2022) for the "memory time" argument; Chinchilla FLOPs (Hoffmann et al., 2022).

CODE
Listing A.1 (p.14) is a PyTorch gist mask, about 10 lines of logic. Core of `make_gist_mask(inputs, gist_token, pad_token)`:
```
pre_gist_mask = make_mask_post_last_gist(inputs, gist_token, dtype=torch.bool)[:, None, None]
post_gist_mask = make_mask_pre_first_gist(inputs, gist_token, dtype=torch.bool)[:, None, None]
pre_gist_time_mask = pre_gist_mask.permute((0, 1, 3, 2))
mask = torch.where(pre_gist_time_mask, pre_gist_mask, post_gist_mask)
mask = mask & (inputs != pad_token)[:, None, None]
```
The helper is `make_mask_pre_first_gist`: `((inputs == gist_token).cumsum(-1) >= 1)`.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): prompting vs finetuning/distillation vs gisting. It shows gisting predicts the cache G(t) from the prompt with no per-task training.
- Fig 2 (p.3): gist mask tables for decoder-only and encoder-decoder models. This is the fastest way to see the method.
- Fig 3 (p.6): ROUGE-L and ChatGPT win rate against k in {1, 2, 5, 10}, with compression factors 2x-26x and positive/negative control lines. It shows that k barely matters.
- Fig A.3 (p.19): exact-match rate with the positive control.
- Fig A.4 (p.19): per-layer FLOPs breakdown, with the dense block at 51.9% and kq/softmax terms that depend on the cache at about 9.6%.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The figure axis text extracted as noise, but the numbers come from Table 1, which extracted cleanly. Figure A.2 text is garbled (an encoding artifact) and has no content. Listing A.3 beyond Example 6 was skimmed, not read.

Note for the target note (05-compression-compaction.md): this is learned soft-token compression of an instruction prompt in the model's KV cache. It is not text summarisation or compaction of conversation history. Any citation should say that. It is a sharpens-style citation only if the note already discusses prompt compression.
